title: This Former Intel CEO Wants to Jumpstart Moore’s Law With Light
gist: Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, now a general partner at Playground, argues lithography — not processor design — is the way to restart Moore's law, backing xLight's free-electron-laser push below ASML's 13.5nm wavelength toward 5-2nm. He also calls the $1T semiconductor market five years early, predicts a training-to-inference swing onto non-GPU silicon and stacked memory past HBM, and frames US energy capacity growth (low single digits for a decade) as the real AI constraint, with pre-release model review coming either from industry or government.

themes.theme: Lithography as the Moore's law unlock

insights.claim: Pat Gelsinger argues the impasse in Moore's law breaks through lithography rather than processor design, because every alternative path — new material structures, superconducting, ferroelectric materials — still depends on lithography.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Concentrates the deep-tech semis bet on litho tooling and light sources rather than on architecture startups.
insights.quote: Light is the most important thing.
insights.locator: You think lithography is the key to reawakening Moore’s law

insights.claim: ASML's leading lithography technology prints with 13.5-nanometer wavelength light, and xLight's aim is to push below that to 5-, 4-, 3- or 2-nanometer wavelengths using free-electron lasers.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: A concrete technical target that, if hit, resets the feature-size roadmap and the value of the entire EUV installed base.
insights.quote: Can I move past 13.5-nanometer light? That’s the next breakthrough.
insights.locator: One of the reasons I joined Playground was because of xLight

insights.claim: xLight is positioned as complementary to ASML rather than a competitor, with the first goal being to hook its light source to existing ASML machines to make them better.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: A partner-not-challenger posture means the bull case runs through ASML adoption, not displacement — a very different risk profile for both.
insights.quote: xLight is not versus ASML, it’s with ASML.
insights.locator: xLight is not versus ASML

insights.claim: xLight has recently received investment from the US government, and Gelsinger took a board seat on joining Playground.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Government co-investment in a pre-revenue light-source startup signals where US industrial policy is placing its semiconductor bets after fabs.
insights.locator: he took a board seat at xLight, a portfolio company developing novel lithography

insights.claim: The semiconductor industry's trillion-dollar revenue target, set in 2024 for 2030, will now be reached next year — AI pulled the milestone forward by roughly five years.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: A five-year pull-forward in the TAM is the single number underwriting today's deep-tech and semicap valuations.
insights.quote: In 2024, the semiconductor industry aimed to hit a trillion dollars by 2030. Now, we’ll hit a trillion dollars next year.
insights.locator: The door has blown wide open.

insights.claim: With a market that large, deep tech portfolio companies do not need to win their market to deliver extraordinary returns — winning a decent percentage suffices.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Reframes underwriting for hardware startups: share-capture assumptions can be modest and still clear venture hurdles.
insights.quote: I don’t need my companies to win the market to get extraordinary returns. I just need them to win a decent percentage.
insights.locator: The door has blown wide open.

insights.claim: Most venture firms pivoting into deep tech have forgotten how to do it and can no longer pick winners and losers, which is where an operator-led firm's edge lies.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Predicts dispersion, not uniform returns, in the deep-tech vintage — capital is abundant but selection skill is not.
insights.quote: The bad news is that, for the most part, they’ve forgotten how to do deep tech—how to pick the winners and losers.
insights.locator: A bunch of VCs are shifting toward deep tech

insights.claim: Deep tech diligence at Playground runs on a technical investment team of engineers, PhDs and professors plus interviews and background checks, with the test being whether founders can articulate the hard problem in depth.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: A repeatable screen for evaluating pre-proof hardware teams where financial diligence gives no signal.
insights.quote: We’re looking to fund the best team—not a team—on a given topic.
insights.locator: What’s your process for assessing the credibility of deep tech founders

insights.claim: When a deep tech idea emerges, two or three companies typically gravitate to it, so the investment question is rarely whether the category exists but whether you picked the best team in it.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Category risk is lower than team risk in deep tech — reverses the usual venture framing and changes how to size positions.
insights.quote: Very rarely do you find the dodo bird.
insights.locator: Generally, when you see deep tech things emerge

insights.claim: Gelsinger chose venture over private equity because private equity writes bigger checks but is not as focused on the technology, and he did not want to do more public earnings calls.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Explains why an ex-Intel CEO is now a source of deal flow and diligence signal in early-stage semis rather than a buyout operator.
insights.locator: Why did you decide against private equity?

insights.claim: Gelsinger predicts a swing from training to inference and says that inference will run on chips that do not look like today's GPUs, noting Nvidia itself recognized its GPUs were not a great fit for all inferencing.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: The core structural challenge to Nvidia's moat: the workload mix shifts toward the segment where its architecture is least advantaged.
insights.quote: We train models once, we use them many [times]. There will be a swing toward inference.
insights.locator: What do you make of the wave of semiconductor startups trying to challenge Nvidia

insights.claim: Model vendors are trying to abstract themselves from the underlying hardware to make heterogeneous hardware structures easier underneath.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Abstraction at the model layer is the mechanism that lowers switching costs away from a single accelerator vendor — watch it as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: They’re trying to make it easier to have a heterogeneous hardware structure underneath.
insights.locator: I think that model vendors are trying to abstract themselves

insights.claim: High-bandwidth memory is a problematic technology that is merely the best available now, and stacked memory architectures will become much more dominant by the end of the decade, with d-Matrix, Fractile and Cerebras breaking the boundaries.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: A call that the HBM supply-constraint trade has a defined shelf life, with named challengers to track.
insights.quote: High-bandwidth memory is a problematic technology. It’s the best we have right now.
insights.locator: What about memory?

insights.claim: Gelsinger expects some hardware innovations to be 10 to 100 times better, meaning one gigawatt of power would produce ten gigawatts' worth of tokens.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: If efficiency gains of that scale land, the energy-constrained bull case for datacenter power demand is overstated at the margin.
insights.quote: That means one gigawatt produces 10 gigawatts worth of tokens. I’ll take that deal any day.
insights.locator: I believe that some of these hardware innovations are going to be 10 to 100X better

insights.claim: Gelsinger frames his mandate at Playground as making AI 10,000 times better rather than 10 times, which he says cannot happen on today's GPU designs.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Sets the ambition threshold he screens deals against — useful for reading which startups he will and will not back.
insights.quote: My job at Playground is to make AI 10,000 times better, not 10 times.
insights.locator: Obviously, training has been the heartland of GPUs

themes.theme: Energy as the binding AI constraint

insights.claim: US energy capacity has expanded at only low single digits over the last decade, which Gelsinger calls despicable, arguing that in a digital AI age energy capacity is economic capacity.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: The cleanest statement of the power-first framework for AI infrastructure investing — capacity growth, not generation mix, is the metric.
insights.quote: In a digital AI age, energy capacity is economic capacity.
insights.locator: You’ve previously described energy as one of the main bottlenecks

insights.claim: Gelsinger says climate focus came at the cost of capacity — 'we were so consumed with climate that we forgot about capacity' — while explicitly disclaiming an anti-climate position.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Marks the political shift in how AI-adjacent capital talks about energy policy, which precedes permitting and subsidy changes.
insights.quote: I don’t want to be anti-climate, but we were so consumed with climate that we forgot about capacity.
insights.locator: In the US, we’ve had low-single-digit expansion in energy capacity

insights.claim: Every fast route to new power is blocked: new gas turbines carry an eight-year supply chain, nuclear takes a decade to build, and solar depends on Chinese supply chains.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Quantifies why power is the hard constraint — no supply response is available inside the current AI capex cycle.
insights.quote: New gas turbines have an eight-year supply chain; nuclear takes a decade to build; solar [depends on] Chinese supply chains.
insights.locator: But it’s really a conundrum

insights.claim: Alva Energy, a Gelsinger portfolio company, is doing nuclear upgrading — harvesting more value from the existing nuclear footprint as the fast path while longer-cycle nuclear build restarts.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Uprates of existing reactors are the only near-term nuclear capacity available; a named vehicle for that trade.
insights.quote: Let’s take the fast path—harvesting more value from today’s nuclear footprint—but also let’s reignite the nuclear build.
insights.locator: One of my companies, Alva Energy, is doing nuclear upgrading

insights.claim: Gelsinger asserts the winners and losers of the AI age will be determined by who has the energy capacity to build their systems.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: A single-variable framework for ranking AI competitors that favors incumbents with power contracts over model quality alone.
insights.quote: fundamentally the winners and losers in the AI age will be those with the energy capacity to build their systems
insights.locator: This is an area that needs innovation

insights.claim: The third leg of the energy answer is efficiency across the whole stack, including chips and power distribution, with Playground backing several voltage regulation and conversion companies.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Power conversion and regulation is an under-covered part of the AI datacenter bill of materials that a major investor is actively funding.
insights.locator: The final piece is to make AI a lot more efficient

insights.claim: Gelsinger does not see US technological leadership and even distribution of AI benefits as in conflict, and says if forced to choose between US or Chinese leadership in foundational models he picks the US so models reflect Western values.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: The ideological premise underwriting export controls — held by an investor with government co-investment, so it predicts policy alignment in his portfolio.
insights.quote: This is a race we want Western nations to win.
insights.locator: There’s yin and yang on these types of topics

insights.claim: A major foundational model is being released roughly every four weeks, which Gelsinger says makes it genuinely unclear what and whether to regulate.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Release cadence is the practical reason model-level regulation keeps slipping — assume no binding US framework near term.
insights.quote: A major foundational model is being released every four weeks.
insights.locator: This is just moving so fast.

insights.claim: Gelsinger's stated governance standard is integrity of process and visibility of testing — disclosure of what proprietary foundational models are trained on, vigorous benchmarking, and demonstrated security and values alignment — and he says either industry does that review or government will have to step in.
insights.speaker: Pat Gelsinger
insights.so_what: Frames self-regulation as the industry's last window before mandated pre-release review; watch for a lab-led benchmarking consortium as the tell.
insights.quote: One of two things needs to happen: Either the industry does that review, or the government has to step in to make sure it gets done.
insights.locator: But what’s your stance? Should models be reviewed
